question: What makes unit tests good, and why must test code be kept as clean as production code?

results.claim: Dirty tests are equivalent to, if not worse than, no tests: a coached team's suite became a liability, was discarded, and defects rose.
results.setup: One anecdote of a team Martin coached; no data given
results.quote: having dirty tests is equivalent to, if not worse than, having no tests

results.claim: Test code is as important as production code and must be kept as clean.
results.quote: Test code is just as important as production code.

results.claim: Tests enable change, so they keep code flexible, maintainable and reusable; higher coverage means less fear of change.
results.quote: Tests enable all the -ilities, because tests enable change.

results.claim: A clean test is above all readable; the refactor from Listing 9-1 to 9-2 uses build-operate-check structure and a test-specific helper language.
results.quote: Three things. Readability, readability, and readability.

results.claim: Test code follows a dual standard: it may be less efficient (memory, CPU) than production code but never less clean.
results.setup: getState string concatenation in MockControlHardware (Listing 9-6), embedded controller example
results.quote: But they never involve issues of cleanliness.

results.claim: One assert per test is a good guideline but Martin accepts multiple asserts; the better rule is one concept per test.
results.setup: SerialDate addMonths example (Listing 9-8) split into three concepts; reveals a missing Feb 28 test
results.quote: you should minimize the number of asserts per concept and test just one concept per test function.

results.claim: Clean tests are F.I.R.S.T.: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely.
results.quote: Clean tests follow five other rules that form the above acronym

limits: Anecdote and assertion only; no measurements or data.
Martin concedes the chapter only scratches the surface: an entire book could be written about clean tests (p. 133).
Java examples; written 2008 and predates mocking-framework critiques, so it says little about test doubles, test sizes, flakiness, coverage targets or mutation testing.
Written against JUnit 4 style; the one-assert school cites a 2005 blog.
practices: Follow the three laws of TDD: no production code without a failing test, no more test than needed to fail, no more production code than needed to pass (p. 122).
Keep test code to the same cleanliness standard as production code (p. 124).
Structure tests as build, operate, check (p. 127).
Build a domain-specific testing language by refactoring test code, not designing it up front (p. 127).
Allow tests to be less efficient than production code but never less clean (pp. 127-130).
Minimise asserts per test and test one concept per test function (pp. 130-132).
Use given-when-then names for single-assert tests (p. 130).
Mock out timing functions to control time in tests of time-dependent code (p. 122).
Write tests just before the production code so the code is designed to be testable (p. 133).
Make tests runnable in any order and in any environment, including offline, and pass/fail without reading logs (p. 132).

terms.definition: You may not write production code until you have written a failing unit test; not write more of a unit test than sufficient to fail; not write more production code than sufficient to pass the failing test.
Each test builds up the test data, operates on it, then checks that the operation yielded the expected results.
A set of functions and utilities over the programmer-facing APIs that makes tests convenient to write and easy to read.
Test-support code need not be as efficient as production code but must stay simple, succinct and expressive.
